tracks.title: One shift, under the cover
tracks.text: Lesson five point one — loops. A sub-lesson, under agents. [curious] Agent is the most hand-waved word in software. The parent lesson hired the worker — files, a schedule, memory, tenure. Fine. But this lesson opens the engine cover on a single shift. When that worker works for twenty minutes… what is actually executing? Why doesn't it hang forever? And when it does something strange at two in the morning… what can you actually read back? In most frameworks the answer is a shrug wrapped in a diagram. Here it's shorter, and less flattering to the word agent. A run is one recursive function — about fifty lines — and you can read all of them.

tracks.title: The run, defined
tracks.text: The run, defined. One trip around — model… to tools… to append — repeated until the model stops asking for tools, signals done, or spends its step budget. And it returns a small record — a result, a step count, the events, and the log. One word in that definition carries the weight… step. A step is one model turn that called tools. So if the model asks for three tools in a single turn, that's three tool calls sharing one step number. The counter bumps once per trip around the loop — not once per tool. Twelve steps means the model was consulted twelve times… not that twelve things happened. Hold onto that. The whole trace reads off it.

tracks.title: One trip around the loop
tracks.text: One trip around the loop. Here is the entire machine — picture it as a wheel. The run seeds the transcript with two messages — the system prompt, and the user's task — and then it spins. Each pass does one thing… ask the model, and branch on the answer. So follow the wheel. First, it asks the model — one turn. Then a fork. Did it call tools? If no tool calls came back, the run finishes — the model's text becomes the result, and we're done. If tool calls did come back, run every one of them — each under a hundred-and-fifty-second guillotine — then a second fork. Was one of them the done tool, or did something error? If it was done, finish, and hand back done's result. If neither, append the assistant message and the tool results to the transcript… add one to the step count… and ask whether we've hit the budget. If step is at the max, finish with a string — stopped, reached max steps. Otherwise — back to the top of the wheel, ask the model again. And hanging off the side, one more arrow… an L-L-M error on any turn finishes the run with a string that starts with error… never a crash. [curious] So trace the exits. Two are clean — the model stops asking, or the model calls done. Two carry a string — the step cap, and the error. That's the whole philosophy in one line… a run never crashes out. Failure becomes the result. No planner. No graph engine. [excited] The transcript is the state, and that wheel is all of it.

tracks.title: What the model actually sees
tracks.text: What the model actually sees — a depth rung, skip it if the wheel was enough. The reason there's no hidden state is that the transcript is the state. A flat list of messages you could print. Picture the conversation as a sequence. The loop sends the model the messages plus the tool specs. The model sends back an assistant message and some tool calls. The loop runs each call against the tools, gets the outputs back — each clipped to four thousand characters — then appends the assistant message and the results, and adds one to the step. Then it sends the model the longer transcript… again. This time the model replies with no tool calls and some text — and with no calls, the loop finishes. That back-and-forth is how the model remembers what its last tool returned. It doesn't, really. The loop hands it back. Two housekeeping facts keep it honest. First, assistant messages are stripped down to just role, content, and tool calls before they're kept — nothing else rides along. Second, tool outputs are truncated to four thousand characters going in, so a chatty tool can't blow out the context. The turn itself is one call to OpenRouter — default model is mimo, overridable per run or by environment variable, temperature nought point four. And the key lives host-side. The agent never sees it. Secrets are held by reference… not handed into the loop.

tracks.title: Nothing waits forever
tracks.text: Nothing waits forever — this is the section that earns the word engine. Every tool call runs inside a killable task. It starts the task, then yields for a hundred and fifty seconds… or shuts it down with a brutal kill. In plain terms — the tool gets a hundred and fifty seconds, and if it doesn't return, it dies. And here's what makes it more than a timeout. When a tool is killed, the model's next context contains, as an ordinary tool result, a line that reads — tool error, git timed out after a hundred and fifty seconds, killed. [curious] A timeout is not an exception that unwinds the run. It's a string the model reads on its next turn… and reacts to. Retry. Work around. File an issue. The run never stalls. Now the war story. The L-L-M call itself was also seen to hang — runs stuck for ten minutes inside a single completion — because the H-T-T-P client's own timeout was watched, and seen not to fire. [sighs] So the model turn sits inside a second kill-bound. A hundred and twenty seconds per request, up to two retries, and a hard outer deadline of three hundred and seventy-five seconds… after which the whole completion is killed. Two guillotines, one inside the other. There's a table of every bound, and here's its verdict in a breath. [curious] A tool gets a hundred and fifty seconds. The model turn gets that three-seventy-five outer bound. The run gets a step budget — twelve by default, but every real surface raises it. A fetch gets twenty seconds. And image generation gets two attempts a run. Each breach hands the model a string it can read — never a stall. And that step budget — the default twelve is a floor nobody experiences. The H-T-T-P endpoint defaults to forty. The keeper, sixty. The autopoet, eighty. One ask endpoint runs to two hundred and fifty. And a workflow component is held to a tight six. The budget belongs to the caller… not the loop.

tracks.title: Nine tools, and three you earn
tracks.text: Nine tools — and three you earn. Every agent gets the same nine base tools, and none of them is a way to run an arbitrary command on the host — that hatch was removed on purpose. There's a table of the surface, and here's the shape of it. The base nine — shell, search, fetch, web search, wb, file issue, vfs read and write, and done. Three more — git, publish, and image — are host-brokered, and granted only to trusted agents. The pattern across every row is the same… the agent supplies intent, the host runs a fixed operation. And done is a tool too, not magic — calling it is just how the model says, I'm finished, here's the result. Two rows hide a real story. First, shell — it speaks pipes, and and-or with short-circuit, variables, redirection — but there is no operating-system process behind it. Each stage is a wasm instance. And it treats a redirect to dev-null as a silent no-op instead of an error… which sounds trivial until you learn it was once the single biggest source of a production agent's per-run thrash. Second, image — its budget of two is spent on attempt, not on success. A failed generation still burns a slot, and the message tells the agent — plan your banners, don't spray.

tracks.title: Brokered, not bestowed
tracks.text: Brokered, not bestowed — another depth rung. The host runs git for you sounds like native shell access with extra steps. [chuckles] It isn't. And the difference is the whole trust model. The agent can never choose a command line. For git, it supplies a commit message and nothing else — the host decides it's a commit-and-push, against this workdir, for this tenant. There is no string the agent can write that becomes a delete on the host… because there's no place to write it. And this is enforced, not promised. The old native-exec hatch — a generic run tool, an operating-system sandbox wrapper — was deleted. And a test stands guard so it can't quietly come back. It reads, plainly — there is no run tool on the base surface, and none on the exec surface… the native sandbox module is gone… and native compiler fallbacks must error, not execute. The other half of trust is containment. Even a trusted agent's file paths must resolve strictly inside its workdir — a path that escapes returns, write blocked, path escapes your working dir. Without that guard, an exec agent could read the host's password file, the engine's own source, or another tenant's repo. That's the hole that would make any confined-to-the-config-layer claim a lie. And a non-exec agent that tries git gets — git not permitted, no exec capability. Notice — that's a tool result the model reads… not an error thrown at a caller. The permission is part of the conversation.

tracks.title: The run narrates itself, three ways
tracks.text: The run narrates itself — three ways. You should never have to guess what a run did. By construction it leaves three records, at three speeds. Picture one step event — it carries the step number, which agent, the tool, its arguments, the output, an exit code, an error slot, a duration in milliseconds, and a timestamp. That one event fans out to three sinks. First — live. A callback pushes WebSocket frames as it goes… a step frame per step, then a final done frame. Second — always-on. One J-S-O-N line per step is appended to a file called underscore steps dot jsonl, output clipped to two hundred characters, lock-free… and this one is written regardless of what the caller asked for. Nothing escapes by construction. Even the write failing is swallowed rather than disrupting the run. Third — at finish. The events are rendered into an org-mode document. And that middle layer is load-bearing, not decorative. Three things downstream read those raw lines. The signed ledger hash-chains them and signs the head. The dream phase digests them. And the public activity wire groups them by the agent tag. Let me read you one real step, both ways. The jsonl line — the during-the-run view — says… step three, agent waldo, tool shell, the pipeline cats a file, pipes it through jq for user names, and sorts unique. Output… ada, grace. Exit code zero, no error, four hundred and twelve milliseconds. And the same step at finish, in the org document, reads… headline — step three, shell, tagged tool-call. A properties drawer holding the same pipeline under args. Then the output… ada grace. And below it — a Result heading — published the roster page. Watch the truncations as you cross the layers… two hundred characters in the jsonl, three hundred in the org body, four thousand in the transcript the model saw. The trace is a faithful skeleton — not a byte-perfect recording. And the agent field stamps every line with who did the work.

tracks.title: Every failure becomes text
tracks.text: Every failure becomes text — the loop's whole failure philosophy, in one place. Nothing here throws the run off the rails. Each failure lands in the transcript as a string the model reads on its next turn, and that you read later in the trace. A run always ends with a result. There's a table of failures, and here's its verdict. Malformed tool arguments come back as a required-arg-missing string. A tool past a hundred and fifty seconds — timed out, killed. The image budget spent — exhausted, two a run. No exec capability — git not permitted. A path that escapes — write blocked. The L-L-M errors — the run finishes with error. And running out of steps — the run finishes with stopped, reached max steps. Every one… a string, not a crash. And the most interesting one isn't really a failure of the loop — it's the agent admitting it hit a wall. File issue is a tool. When an agent's equipment falls short — my toolkit lacks a verb for this — it files a metacognitive ticket, and the reply tells it to note it and carry on, rather than stall. The wall becomes a tool call, the run keeps moving, and the autopoet picks the ticket up later. Hitting a limit is, itself… just another line in the transcript.

tracks.title: Honesty
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what this machine is, and what it deliberately isn't. [curious] First, a step budget is a budget… not judgment. A run that hits the cap stops mid-thought with a literal stopped-reached-max-steps. It doesn't summarize, doesn't wrap up gracefully. The number is a leash, not intelligence. Second, a hundred and fifty seconds kills slow-but-honest work too. A legitimately long tool gets the same guillotine as a hung one. The bound buys you a run that can't wedge — it costs you the occasional good tool that needed three minutes. Third, truncation is everywhere — four thousand characters in the transcript, about five hundred in a live frame, three hundred in the org, two hundred in the jsonl. The trace records faithfully what happened… not every byte, and not why. Fourth, the org narrative only exists at finish — while a run is live, the during view is the jsonl and the stream. And fifth, trust is binary, and host-granted. An agent is exec or it isn't — it never acquires the grant itself. Capability flows down from the host, never up from the agent. And the framing all of this serves — [curious] this is observability for people building with agents. A trace you can read… a run that can't run away from you. It is never a pitch about software that runs itself. The loop makes the work legible and bounded. It does not make the human optional.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] At the step cap, does it summarize first? No. The guard fires the moment step reaches the max, and the run finishes with the literal stopped string. No wrap-up turn. If you want a clean ending, give the budget room, or prompt the agent to call done near the edge. Can I watch a run live? Yes. The post endpoint returns a two-oh-two immediately, with a running status — the run continues in a supervised process that outlives the caller. Then the stream endpoint is a WebSocket of step frames ending in done… or you poll for status. Can the agent lie in its own trace? The jsonl is written by the host, per step — the agent doesn't author it. Whether someone can tamper with it afterward is a different question, and the answer is the ledger… it hash-chains the raw lines and signs the head, so editing history is detectable. What model runs the loop? Any OpenRouter chat model — the default is mimo, a per-agent definition sets one, an environment variable overrides globally. The loop is model-agnostic. And — can the model call several tools in one step? Yes, and they share one step number. [chuckles] Tool execution reduces over all the calls in a turn without bumping the counter — so a step can carry one call… or five.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's a single shift, under the microscope. A run is one recursive function — model, tools, append — that ends when the model stops asking, signals done, or runs out of steps. Nothing in it waits forever, every failure becomes text, and the whole thing narrates itself three ways without being asked. [curious] The way back up is short. This sat under agents — lesson five — the worker this loop is one shift of. And two live siblings carry it forward… the autopoet, where those file-issue tickets get answered… and the ledger, where the raw trace becomes tamper-evident. Read the loop once, and the rest of the agent shelf is just callers of this one function.
